Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: A Clock That STA Does Not See
  1. clk_i clocks the counter count_q and the divider slow_clk_q, i.e., 25 flip-flops. slow_clk_q clocks only led_q.
  2. Yosys maps the 26 flip-flops onto dfrbpq_1 cells with their reset tied inactive. The netlist has no initial values (Section 3.4.1).
  3. check_setup reports one unclocked register pin, _175_/CLK, the clock pin of led_q, and two unconstrained endpoints, _175_/D and led_o. STA does not check these paths at all: the report shows only the group clk, and a violation behind the divider would go unnoticed.
  4. slow_clk_q toggles every DIV = 12,500,000 cycles, so the generated clock divides clk by 25,000,000 (the file below). check_setup reports nothing anymore. report_clock_properties shows slow_clk with a period of 500,000,000 ns, i.e., 0.5 s, and its edges at 0 and 250,000,000 ns. The new path group slow_clk holds the path to _175_/D. The generated clock is ideal here. In the layout, it also arrives later than clk by the clock-to-output delay of the divider and its own clock tree (Section 3.4.2).
gen_clk/led_blink_fpga.sdc
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Timing constraints of the FPGA LED blinker of chapter
# 3: the 50 MHz clock and the clock that slow_clk_q derives from it.

create_clock -name clk -period 20 [get_ports clk_i]

# slow_clk_q toggles every DIV = 12,500,000 cycles: clk / (2 * DIV)
set div_q [get_pins -of_objects [get_nets slow_clk_q] \
  -filter "direction == output"]
create_generated_clock -name slow_clk -source [get_ports clk_i] \
  -divide_by 25000000 $div_q

set_output_delay 0 -clock clk [all_outputs]
set_load 0.01 [all_outputs]
  1. The ASIC version has one clock, so it needs no generated clock: create_clock at clk_i, an input delay for rst_ni, and the output delay and the load of led_o. Without the input delay, check_setup reports rst_ni as an input without input delay, and the reset paths are not timed. With it, check_setup reports nothing, all 26 flip-flops are in the group clk, and their RESET_B pins in the group asynchronous.

6.9 Timing Exceptions

By default, STA assumes that every path between two registers has one clock period. Timing exceptions change this for selected paths:

  • A false path, set with set_false_path, is removed from the analysis, e.g., a path from a configuration register that is written once and stays constant during operation. Paths between two unrelated clocks also need special treatment (Section 8).
  • A multicycle path, set with set_multicycle_path, gets several clock periods, for logic whose result is only used every few cycles.
  • set_max_delay and set_min_delay set a limit for a path directly, e.g., for a combinational path from an input to an output.

A multicycle path needs care. Run bs_reg with a period of 1.2 ns instead of 4 ns, and the worst setup slack between the registers becomes -0.492 ns. Suppose the RTL loads the input and the output register only every second cycle, with an enable, so that the barrel shifter has two periods. The exception for the setup check is:

set_multicycle_path 2 -setup \
  -from [all_registers] -to [all_registers]

The setup slack becomes 0.708 ns, but the hold check now fails with -0.953 ns. By default, the hold check uses the edge one period before the setup capture edge. Moving the setup edge by one period also moves the hold edge, so the new data must not reach FF2 until one period after the launch edge. The second exception moves the hold edge back to the launch edge:

set_multicycle_path 1 -hold \
  -from [all_registers] -to [all_registers]

The hold slack is back at 0.247 ns. The rule is to set -hold to one less than -setup. Every exception is a promise that the tool cannot check: if the RTL does not really wait for the second cycle, the chip fails while the timing report is clean. So keep exceptions few, and check with assertions in the RTL simulation that the design really waits (Section 4.8).

6.10 Hold Violations

Before the layout, the clock is ideal, and the uncertainty is the only margin that the hold check keeps for the skew of the future clock tree. After clock tree synthesis, set_propagated_clock makes STA compute the latency of every register through the buffers of the clock tree. A short path between two registers whose clocks arrive at different times can then fail the hold check. The layout flow repairs such paths after clock tree synthesis by inserting delay into the data path (Section 10). SG13CMOS5L has three delay cells for that, dlygate4sd1_1 to dlygate4sd3_1, with increasing delay.

A setup violation and a hold violation are fixed in opposite ways. A setup violation needs a shorter path: stronger cells, different logic, a pipeline register (Section 7), or a slower clock. A hold violation needs a longer shortest path or less skew, and the added delay must not break the setup check of the same path.

TipExercise: Fix a Hold Violation

All commands start in the folder content/sequential/code/hold. The netlist shift.v holds two flip-flops in a row, as in a shift register. The clock reaches ff1 directly and ff2 through four buf_1 cells. The script hold.tcl propagates the clock through them and reports the hold and the setup check of the path from ff1 to ff2.

  1. Draw the circuit with its clock path, and mark the clock edges that the hold check compares. Write the hold condition of this path with the delay of the four buffers. How large may their sum be before the check fails?
  2. Run the analysis in the fast, the typical, and the slow corner: CORNER=fast_1p32V_m40C sta -no_init -exit hold.tcl, then with typ_1p20V_25C and slow_1p08V_125C. Which corner has the worst hold slack? Explain it with the numbers of the report.
  3. Run the slow corner with a clock period of 40 ns instead of 4 ns: PERIOD=40 CORNER=slow_1p08V_125C sta -no_init -exit hold.tcl. What changes?
  4. Fix the violation: copy shift.v to shift_orig.v, and insert a sg13cmos5l_dlygate4sd1_1 with the pins A and X between ff1 and ff2. Run all three corners again. Is the hold check met everywhere, and what does the delay cell cost the setup check?

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: Fix a Hold Violation

  1. The hold check compares the launch of ff1 at a clock edge with the capture of ff2 at the same edge, which reaches ff2 later by the delay \(t_\text{buf}\) of the four buffers, the skew. The data path is only the clock-to-output delay of ff1, and hold.tcl sets no uncertainty, so the hold condition is \(t_\text{cq} \ge t_\text{hold} + t_\text{buf}\). The buffers may delay the clock by at most \(t_\text{cq} - t_\text{hold}\). The setup check gains the same skew and has almost the whole period.

  2. The hold slack is -0.022 ns in the fast, -0.030 ns in the typical, and -0.054 ns in the slow corner, so the slow corner is the worst. In the fast corner, the four buffers delay the clock by 0.179 ns and ff1 switches after 0.137 ns, in the slow corner after 0.388 ns and 0.288 ns. Both delays roughly double, but the skew is the larger one, so the difference grows from 0.042 to 0.100 ns. The hold time, -0.021 ns in the fast and -0.047 ns in the slow corner, makes up only part of that. The deficit consists of delays, so it grows with the delays of the corner. A hold check in the fast corner alone would have missed the worst case. With a balanced clock tree, where a fixed margin such as the uncertainty dominates, the fast corner is usually the worst.

  3. The hold slack stays at -0.054 ns, and only the setup slack grows from 3.897 ns to 39.897 ns. The clock period does not appear in the hold condition.

  4. The netlist with the delay cell:

    wire q1d;
sg13cmos5l_dlygate4sd1_1 dly (.A(q1), .X(q1d));
sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1 ff2 (.CLK(ck4), .D(q1d), .RESET_B(1'b1),
  .Q(q_o));

    The hold check is now met in all three corners, with a slack of 0.067 ns in the fast, 0.105 ns in the typical, and 0.161 ns in the slow corner. The setup slack drops from 3.962, 3.941, and 3.897 ns to 3.881, 3.809, and 3.697 ns, i.e., by 0.08 to 0.20 ns, which a path with four nanoseconds to spare can easily afford.

6.11 Latches and Time Borrowing

A latch in a path does not cut it at a fixed time, as a flip-flop does. The netlist borrow/borrow_latch.v has a latch dllrq_1 in the middle of a path from ff1 to ff2, transparent while the clock is low. Six delay cells stand for the logic in front of it, two for the logic behind it. The latch opens at the falling edge, in the middle of the period of 4 ns, and closes at the next rising edge. Data that arrives while the latch is open passes through at once. The time that the first stage uses after the opening edge is borrowed from the second stage. In borrow/borrow_ff.v, a flip-flop on the falling edge of the clock takes the place of the latch:

cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/sequential/code/borrow
TOP=borrow_ff sta -no_init -exit borrow.tcl
TOP=borrow_latch sta -no_init -exit borrow.tcl

With the flip-flop, the first stage has half a period and fails with a slack of -0.474 ns, while the second stage has 1.001 ns to spare. With the latch, OpenSTA reports that the first stage borrows 0.354 ns, and it reports a slack of 0 for the borrowing stage. The second stage starts 0.354 ns later, and the latch passes the data from D to Q a little more slowly than the flip-flop from its clock to Q, so the second stage keeps 0.620 ns of slack. The most a stage can borrow is the transparent phase minus the setup time of the latch.

Time borrowing lets latch-based designs balance their stages automatically, which is why some high-performance processors use latches. The price is a more complex timing analysis, harder hold checks, because a latch launches data already at its opening edge while the next latch holds its data until its closing edge, and a more difficult scan test (Section 9). The designs of this course use flip-flops only.

6.12 Summary

  • A latch is transparent while its gate is active. A flip-flop, built from a master and a slave latch, samples its input at the clock edge. Synchronous designs use flip-flops, so that every register-to-register path has exactly one period.
  • A flip-flop has a clock-to-output delay, a setup and a hold time around the clock edge, a recovery and a removal time for the release of its asynchronous reset, and minimum pulse widths. The library gives them as tables over the slews. Hold times can be negative.
  • The setup condition \(t_\text{cq} + t_\text{logic,max} + t_\text{su} \le T + t_\text{skew} - t_\text{unc}\) sets the clock frequency. The hold condition \(t_\text{cq} + t_\text{logic,min} \ge t_\text{hold} + t_\text{skew} + t_\text{unc}\) does not contain the period, so for a path between flip-flops on the same edge, a lower clock frequency does not fix a hold violation.
  • Static timing analysis propagates arrival times through all paths of the netlist and compares them with required times, without stimuli. It knows nothing about the function, and it checks only what the constraints describe.
  • SDC constraints define the clocks with their transition and uncertainty, generated clocks, the input and output delays of the environment, the driving cells and loads, and timing exceptions. check_setup finds what they forgot. A multicycle path for setup needs a matching one for hold.
  • OpenSTA reports each path with its arrival time, required time, and slack. With its high-fanout nets buffered, the barrel shifter between two registers reaches 591 MHz between its registers in the typical corner, and the release of its reset limits the block to 494 MHz.
  • Hold violations come from clock skew on short paths. Delay cells in the data path fix them, and hold must be checked in all corners.
  • A latch lets a slow stage borrow time from the next one, at the price of a more complex analysis.

In Section 7, we use these reports to make a design faster, smaller, and less power-hungry: pipelining, retiming, resource sharing, and clock gating.

7 Synthesis Optimizations and Low-Power Design

In Section 5, Yosys and ABC mapped RTL onto the cells of the library, and Section 6 measured how fast the result runs. This chapter asks how a design becomes faster, smaller, and less power-hungry, and who does the work. Synthesis does part of it on its own: it picks an adder architecture, shares operators, restructures and sizes the logic, and it can even switch off clocks. The rest is the job of the designer: the architecture, the pipeline, and the decision which registers may sleep. We measure every step with the tools of the earlier chapters and add a new one, the power analysis of OpenSTA.

Note

All code of this chapter is available in the folder content/synth_opt/code of the course repository: adders between registers in adder/, two multipliers in share/, a register with an enable in clock_gate/, and the constraints and scripts that all of them use in syn/. All numbers in this chapter come from the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS image 2026.10 (Yosys 0.70, OpenSTA 3.1.0, Icarus Verilog 14.0) and the standard-cell library of SG13CMOS5L, in the typical corner unless a corner is named. The script scripts/check_synth_opt.sh reproduces all of them: run bash scripts/check_synth_opt.sh in the container from the root of the repository.

For the exercises, clone the course repository into your designs folder once, if you have not done so yet:

cd /foss/designs
git clone https://github.com/iic-jku/vlsi-design.git

In every new terminal, define the path of the typical-corner library and of the ABC constraint file of Section 5.7:

LIB=$PDK_ROOT/ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell/lib
LIB=$LIB/sg13cmos5l_stdcell_typ_1p20V_25C.lib

CONSTR=$CONSTR/synth/abc.constr

7.1 Learning Objectives

After this chapter, you will be able to:

  • tell which optimizations logic synthesis performs on the operators and on the gates, and which ones remain the job of the designer
  • compare the ripple-carry adder with parallel-prefix adders, and select the adder architecture in Yosys
  • explain resource sharing, and check whether synthesis has shared an operator
  • shorten the critical path with a pipeline register, and explain retiming
  • name the components of the power consumption of a CMOS circuit and the levers that reduce them
  • estimate the power of a netlist with OpenSTA, with and without the activity of a simulation
  • explain why clock gating needs an integrated clock gate, and insert one with Yosys

7.2 What Synthesis Optimizes

An optimization can act on three levels:

  • The architecture. The algorithm, how many operations run in parallel, how many clock cycles a result takes, the number of pipeline stages, the memories, and the number formats are decisions of the designer. Synthesis keeps the registers of the RTL, apart from re-encoding state machines, removing unused or duplicate registers (Section 5.8), and retiming, which runs only on request (Section 7.5). A design that computes its result in one clock cycle still does so after synthesis, and a serial design stays serial. No synthesis tool turns a bubble sort into a quicksort.
  • The operators. Yosys works on the operators of the RTL first. It folds constants and removes unused logic (opt, opt_clean), extracts state machines and may re-encode them (fsm), shrinks operators to the widths that are really used (wreduce), merges identical cells (opt_merge), collects additions and multiplications into arithmetic cells (alumacc), shares operators (share, opt_share), and finally builds every operator from gates with one of the templates of its library (techmap).
  • The gates. ABC restructures the gates of each combinational block between the registers, maps them onto the cells of the library, and sizes and buffers them (Section 5.7). It runs twice in the commands of this course: synth ends with an abc pass that maps onto generic gates, and the command abc -liberty maps onto the library. Only the Boolean function of the block counts, so in principle ABC may rebuild a block completely. Its algorithms work on small windows of the logic, though, and they start from the structure that Yosys hands over.

Several of these steps have switches, both in Yosys and in LibreLane, the RTL-to-GDSII flow of Section 10 (Table 33).

The synth command of Yosys runs the passes arith_tree and booth only on request, while LibreLane runs both by default. LibreLane maps with the strategy AREA 0 by default, and the counter of the AMS chip template uses DELAY 4. The following sections go through the optimizations one by one.

7.3 Adders

An adder computes for every bit \(i\) a generate \(g_i = a_i b_i\), which is 1 if the bit produces a carry by itself, and a propagate \(p_i = a_i \oplus b_i\), which is 1 if the bit passes an incoming carry on. The sum bit is \(s_i = p_i \oplus c_i\), with the carry \(c_{i+1} = g_i + p_i c_i\) into the next bit. Adders differ only in how they compute the carries.

The ripple-carry adder computes \(c_{i+1}\) from \(c_i\), one bit after the other. It is the smallest adder, one full adder per bit, but the carry passes through all \(n\) bits, so its delay grows linearly with \(n\). Written out bit by bit, it looks like this (adder/rtl/add_ripple.sv):

assign c[0] = 1'b0;
for (genvar i = 0; i < WIDTH; i++) begin : g_fa
  assign s[i]   = a_q[i] ^ b_q[i] ^ c[i];
  assign c[i+1] = (a_q[i] & b_q[i]) | (c[i] & (a_q[i] ^ b_q[i]));
end

A parallel-prefix adder combines the bits into groups. A group generates a carry if its upper part generates one, or if its upper part propagates and its lower part generates one. It propagates a carry if both parts propagate. For the generate \(G\) and the propagate \(P\) of two adjacent groups, the prefix operator \(\circ\) gives those of the combined group:

\[(G_h, P_h) \circ (G_l, P_l) = (G_h + P_h G_l,\ P_h P_l)\]

The carry out of bit \(i\) is the generate of the group of bits 0 to \(i\). Since the operator is associative, the groups can be combined in any grouping, e.g., in a tree with \(\log_2 n\) levels instead of a chain of \(n - 1\). Figure 26 compares three carry networks for 8 bits.

The prefix trees trade the number of operators, the wiring, and the fanout against the number of levels:

  • Kogge-Stone: \(\log_2 n\) levels with \(n \log_2 n - n + 1\) operators. Every operator drives at most two others, but the network has many long wires.
  • Brent-Kung: \(2 \log_2 n - 1\) levels with only \(2n - 2 - \log_2 n\) operators.
  • Sklansky: \(\log_2 n\) levels with \(\frac{n}{2} \log_2 n\) operators, but the fanout doubles from level to level, up to \(n/2\) on the last level.
  • Han-Carlson: Kogge-Stone on every second bit and one more level for the bits in between, i.e., \(\log_2 n + 1\) levels with fewer operators than Kogge-Stone.

For 32 bits, the ripple-carry adder has 31 operators on 31 levels, Brent-Kung 57 operators on 9 levels, and Kogge-Stone 129 operators on 5 levels. Weste and Harris treat these and further adder architectures in depth (Weste and Harris 2010).

Yosys turns + and - into an $alu cell, and techmap builds its carries with a lookahead carry unit $lcu, by default as a Brent-Kung tree (the module _90_lcu_brent_kung in techmap.v). The folder choices of Yosys holds three alternatives, which synth -extra-map selects: synth -extra-map +/choices/kogge-stone.v, and in the same way sklansky.v and han-carlson.v, where +/ stands for the data folder of Yosys. LibreLane has no switch for these prefix adders: its variable SYNTH_ADDER_TYPE only selects full-adder, ripple-carry, or carry-select adders from mapping files that the PDK must provide, and SG13CMOS5L provides none.

A sum of more than two operands, e.g., a + b + c + d, needs no chain of adders. A row of full adders adds three numbers into two, a sum and a carry vector, without passing a carry from bit to bit. A tree of such carry-save adders reduces any number of operands to two, and one final adder adds them. A multiplier works the same way: it sums its partial products, one per bit of one operand, in such a tree. Booth encoding halves the number of partial products. Yosys builds a carry-save tree for every $macc_v2 cell, i.e., for a sum of more than two operands and for the partial products of a multiplier (the pass maccmap). synth -arith_tree replaces these trees by trees of 4:2 compressors and also merges chains of separate adders, and synth -booth builds Booth multipliers.

TipExercise: Ripple or Prefix?

All commands start in the folder content/synth_opt/code/adder. The modules add_reg and add_ripple add two 32-bit numbers between an input and an output register, add_reg with + and add_ripple with the full adders written out.

  1. Draw the prefix graphs of a 16-bit Brent-Kung and a 16-bit Kogge-Stone adder in the style of Figure 26. Count their operators and levels, and check your counts with the formulas.

  2. Synthesize add_ripple with the buffering and sizing of Section 5.7, and run the timing script:

    cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/synth_opt/code/adder
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv rtl/add_ripple.sv; \
  synth -top add_ripple; dfflibmap -liberty $LIB; \

TOP=add_ripple sta -no_init -exit ../syn/sta.tcl

For each adder, note the area, the minimum period between the registers, and the number of cells on the worst path between the two flip-flops. Which adder is the fastest, and what does it cost? In each design, the 97 flip-flops take 4752 µm² of the area.

    yosys -p "read_verilog -sv rtl/add_reg.sv; \

    Repeat it with synth -top add_reg -noabc, which skips the abc pass at the end of synth. Then map all three adders without that pass and with the script ../syn/keep.abc, i.e., the script of abc -constr without its first steps &fraig -x, scorr, dc2, and dretime: use synth -noabc and replace abc -constr $CONSTR by abc -script ../syn/keep.abc -constr $CONSTR. What do you see?

  5. Does the adder architecture of the RTL survive synthesis? What follows for writing arithmetic in RTL?

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: Ripple or Prefix?

  1. The Brent-Kung adder has \(2 \cdot 16 - 2 - 4 = 26\) operators on \(2 \cdot 4 - 1 = 7\) levels: 8, 4, 2, and 1 operators on the way up to bit 15, then 1, 3, and 7 on the way back down to the bits in between. The Kogge-Stone adder has \(16 \cdot 4 - 16 + 1 = 49\) operators on 4 levels: 15, 14, 12, and 8 operators, which combine each bit with the bit 1, 2, 4, and 8 positions to the right.

  2. The results of steps 2 to 4:

    Adder Mapping Cells Area (µm²) Period Cells on path
    ripple-carry -constr 254 6462.9 4.74 ns 32
    Brent-Kung -constr 264 6448.4 3.83 ns 32
    Kogge-Stone -constr 293 6753.0 3.30 ns 27
    ripple-carry keep.abc 239 6372.2 4.78 ns 32
    Brent-Kung keep.abc 294 6809.4 2.11 ns 10
    Kogge-Stone keep.abc 413 7923.4 1.45 ns 7
    ripple-carry delay.abc 370 7580.3 2.03 ns 10
    Brent-Kung delay.abc 379 7741.7 2.78 ns 17
    Kogge-Stone delay.abc 363 7516.9 2.06 ns 12

    With the mapping of Section 5.7 (step 2), the Kogge-Stone adder is the fastest, with 3.30 ns. Without the flip-flops, it needs 2001 µm², 18 % more than Brent-Kung with 1696 µm². The ripple-carry adder needs about the same area as Brent-Kung and is 24 % slower. Its worst path passes a nand2_2 and then 31 alternating a21oi_2 and o21ai_1 cells, one per bit, i.e., the carry chain \(c_{i+1} = g_i + p_i c_i\) in inverting form. The worst paths of the prefix adders pass 32 and 27 cells, many more than the levels of their trees.

  3. After synth -noabc, the longest path of add_reg passes 18 generic gates, after synth 62, almost as many as the 63 of the ripple-carry adder (Kogge-Stone: 11 and 42). The abc pass at the end of synth flattens the trees: its default script contains dc2, which rewrites the logic for fewer gates and does not keep its depth. The script of abc -constr runs the same steps again, so synth -noabc alone does not help: with abc -constr, the prefix adders still need 3.73 and 3.45 ns. Without these steps, the trees survive, and the textbook order appears: ripple-carry 4.78 ns with 32 cells on its path, Brent-Kung 2.11 ns with 10, and Kogge-Stone 1.45 ns with 7. Kogge-Stone is now 3.3 times as fast as the ripple-carry adder, and its logic twice as large (3172 against 1620 µm²).

  4. With the delay-oriented script, all three adders become faster and larger than with -constr. The ripple-carry adder is now about as fast as Kogge-Stone (2.03 against 2.06 ns), with 10 cells on its worst path, among them wide gates such as nor4_1 and or4_1, and Brent-Kung is now the slowest. The script collapses the carry chain into a few levels of wide gates. The adder logic grows by 38 to 76 %, e.g., from 1711 to 2828 µm² for the ripple-carry adder. The result depends on the starting point, though: from the netlists of synth -noabc, the same script gives 2.21, 1.86, and 2.00 ns.

  5. Only if no step throws it away. The default scripts of ABC rewrite the logic for area and flatten the prefix trees. A script that keeps the structure keeps the architecture and gives the fastest adder of all, and a delay-oriented script rebuilds the arithmetic in a way that depends on where it starts. So write arithmetic with its operators, + instead of full adders, select the architecture and the script with the options of the tools, and compare the results with STA. In this flow, ABC never moves logic across a register: it only sees the logic between the flip-flops (Section 7.5). For more speed than the best mapping gives, the adder needs a pipeline.

7.4 Resource Sharing

Two operations that are never needed in the same clock cycle can share one operator. Multiplexers in front of the operator then select its operands. The module share/rtl/mul_sel.sv registers four 16-bit operands and computes one of two products:

p_o <= sel_q ? a_q * b_q : c_q * d_q;

As written, this line describes two multipliers with a multiplexer behind them. The module share/rtl/mul_sel_shared.sv selects the operands first and multiplies them in a single multiplier:

p_o <= x * y;
...
assign x = sel_q ? a_q : c_q;
assign y = sel_q ? b_q : d_q;

Synthesized as in step 2 of the exercise above, i.e., with abc -constr $CONSTR, mul_sel needs 35,237 µm² and a minimum period of 5.25 ns, mul_sel_shared 20,282 µm² and 5.38 ns. Sharing saves 42 % of the area, and the multiplexers in front of the multiplier add 0.13 ns to the path.

Why did Yosys not share the multipliers of mul_sel itself? The command synth runs the pass share, which proves with a formal solver (a solver for Boolean satisfiability, SAT) that two operations are never active in the same cycle and then merges them. In Yosys 0.70, however, alumacc runs before share and turns each multiplication into a $macc_v2 cell, which share does not consider. synth -top mul_sel -run :fine followed by stat shows the two $macc_v2 cells. With synth -noalumacc, the two $mul cells reach share, which merges them into one, with 20,251 µm² and 5.40 ns. For adders, share considers $alu cells only with its option -aggressive. One special case works without help: opt_share merges two operators with a common operand, e.g., sel ? a + b : a + c becomes a + (sel ? b : c).

The lesson is to write the sharing into the RTL where it matters, and to check with stat what synthesis built. Sharing costs multiplexers and their delay, and it only works for operations that are really never needed at the same time. The opposite, duplicating an operator or a register to shorten a path or to reduce a large fanout, is a common timing fix.

7.5 Pipelining and Retiming

The setup condition of Section 6.4 gives a register-to-register path the minimum period \(T_\text{min} = t_\text{cq} + t_\text{logic,max} + t_\text{su} - t_\text{skew} + t_\text{unc}\). ABC can only shorten the logic between the registers. A pipeline register splits the logic into stages, each of which has a full clock period (Figure 27 (a)). With \(k\) stages of equal delay,

\[T_\text{min} = t_\text{cq} + \frac{t_\text{logic,max}}{k} + t_\text{su} - t_\text{skew} + t_\text{unc}.\]

The pipeline delivers one result per clock cycle at a higher clock frequency, i.e., a higher throughput, but every result appears \(k - 1\) cycles later than without the pipeline, i.e., the latency grows. The price is the pipeline registers, their area and their clock power (Section 7.6). The overhead \(t_\text{cq} + t_\text{su} + t_\text{unc}\) of each stage limits the gain: with the values of Table 32 and an uncertainty of 0.1 ns, no stage can be clocked with a period below about 0.43 ns.

The work of pipelining is in the details. Every signal that belongs to the same operation must pass the same number of registers, also an operand that is only used in a later stage, such as x in the figure, and the control signals that travel along, such as a valid flag. Every testbench and every block that uses the result must expect it later.

Retiming moves registers across combinational logic without changing the behavior at the outputs (Figure 27 (b)), e.g., to balance the stages of a pipeline that is cut at the wrong place. Retiming can change the number of registers, it must compute new reset or initial values for the registers it moves, and it breaks the matching of the registers by name in equivalence checking (Section 5.8). Commercial synthesis tools retime on request. In the open-source flow, Yosys passes flip-flops to ABC only with abc -dff (in LibreLane SYNTH_ABC_DFF, off by default), and only flip-flops without a reset: yosys -h abc lists $_DFF_?_ and $_DFFE_??_. Every default script of ABC then runs dretime, which by default retimes for minimum area, i.e., it moves registers to reduce their number, not the delay. Only with a delay target, abc -dff -D <ps>, does ABC add a delay-oriented retime. And abc -dff must run before dfflibmap, while the flip-flops are still generic cells. The designs of this course use flip-flops with an asynchronous reset and place their pipeline registers in the RTL.

    iverilog -g2012 -o sim.vvp rtl/add_pipe.sv tb/tb_add_pipe.sv
vvp -n sim.vvp

    The testbench applies new random operands in every clock cycle and expects each sum three clock edges later. Its first operands, 32'hffffffff and 1, need the carry from the first into the second stage.

  3. Synthesize add_pipe with the commands of the previous exercise, i.e., with abc -constr $CONSTR, and run TOP=add_pipe sta -no_init -exit ../syn/sta.tcl. Compare the cells, the area, the flip-flops, and the minimum period between the registers with add_reg. Estimate the period of add_pipe from the one of add_reg with the formula for \(k\) stages and the overhead of 0.43 ns, and compare it with the measured period. Where is the worst path, and what explains the difference?

  4. report_clock_min_period -include_port_paths reports a longer period for add_pipe, but not for add_reg. Which path sets it, and why does it matter only after pipelining? Hint: copy ../syn/sta.tcl to ../syn/all.tcl, so that it still finds block.sdc, and replace its report_checks command by report_checks -path_delay max -fields {fanout} -digits 3, which reports the worst path of every path group, and run TOP=add_pipe sta -no_init -exit ../syn/all.tcl.

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: Pipeline the Adder
  1. Between the stages, the lower sum with its carry (17 bits) and the upper halves of both operands (2 × 16 bits) need a pipeline register, 49 flip-flops in addition to the 97 of add_reg, 146 in total. The upper halves wait one cycle, so that they meet the carry of their own lower halves. The lower sum waits for the upper sum in the pipeline register.
  2. The module of the reference solution:
adder/rtl/add_pipe.sv
// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: The adder of add_reg in two pipeline stages. Stage 1
// adds the lower halves, stage 2 the upper halves with the carry of
// stage 1. The sum appears one clock cycle later than in add_reg.

`default_nettype none

module add_pipe #(
  parameter int unsigned WIDTH = 32  // even
) (
  input  logic             clk_i,
  input  logic             rst_ni,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] a_i,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] b_i,
  output logic [WIDTH:0]   sum_o
);

  localparam int unsigned H = WIDTH / 2;

  logic [WIDTH-1:0] a_q, b_q;
  logic [H:0]       lo_q;            // lower sum and its carry
  logic [H-1:0]     a_hi_q, b_hi_q;  // upper halves, one stage later
  logic [H:0]       hi;

  // Register process: input register, pipeline register, output
  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) begin
      a_q    <= '0;
      b_q    <= '0;
      lo_q   <= '0;
      a_hi_q <= '0;
      b_hi_q <= '0;
      sum_o  <= '0;
    end else begin
      a_q    <= a_i;
      b_q    <= b_i;
      lo_q   <= a_q[H-1:0] + b_q[H-1:0];
      a_hi_q <= a_q[WIDTH-1:H];
      b_hi_q <= b_q[WIDTH-1:H];
      sum_o  <= {hi, lo_q[H-1:0]};
    end
  end

  // Stage 2: the upper halves and the carry of the lower half
  assign hi = a_hi_q + b_hi_q + lo_q[H];

endmodule

`default_nettype wire

The testbench prints 1000 sums, 0 errors. Without the carry lo_q[H] in the sum of the upper halves, it reports 489 errors. The width of hi matters: as the target of an assignment, the 17-bit hi makes the addition 17 bits wide, so its carry is kept. Inside a concatenation such as {a_hi_q + b_hi_q + lo_q[H], lo_q[H-1:0]}, the sum would only be 16 bits wide.

  1. add_pipe has 303 cells, 8852 µm², and 146 flip-flops, against 264 cells, 6448 µm², and 97 flip-flops of add_reg. Its minimum period is 2.34 ns (427 MHz) instead of 3.83 ns (261 MHz), i.e., it is 1.6 times faster for 37 % more area. The formula predicts \((3.83 - 0.43)/2 + 0.43 = 2.13\) ns. The worst path ends at lo_q[16], the carry out of the first stage, after 17 cells and 2.127 ns, while the 32-bit adder of add_reg needs 32 cells and 3.629 ns. The second stage ends after 2.102 ns, so both stages are about equally long. But each half of the adder needs more than half of the logic delay of the whole adder: 1.90 ns instead of 1.70 ns.
  2. With the port paths, add_pipe needs 2.78 ns. The path is the release of the reset: the driving cell buf_2 of block.sdc needs 1.225 ns to drive the 146 RESET_B pins of rst_ni, and the large slew raises the recovery time to 0.458 ns. With the input delay of 1 ns and the uncertainty, this adds up to 2.78 ns. In add_reg, the same path needs only about 2.3 ns, less than the 3.83 ns between the registers, so it does not show. Pipelining shortened the paths between the registers below the reset path and added 49 loads to the reset net. In the layout flow, the reset net gets a buffer tree (Section 6.7, Section 10).

7.6 Power Consumption

A CMOS circuit consumes power in three ways:

  • Switching power. A transition from 0 to 1 at a net charges its capacitance \(C\), i.e., the inputs of the cells that the net drives and its wire, from the supply, and a transition from 1 to 0 discharges it to ground. On average, each transition dissipates \(\frac{1}{2} C V^2\). With the activity \(a\), the average number of transitions per clock cycle, a net dissipates \(P_\text{sw} = \frac{1}{2} a C V^2 f\) at the supply voltage \(V\) and the clock frequency \(f\). The clock toggles twice per cycle, \(a = 2\), more than any data net without glitches.
  • Internal power. Inside a cell, internal nodes switch as well, and during an edge, the pull-up and the pull-down network both conduct for a short time. The Liberty file gives the energy of each transition at a pin, the internal_power of Section 5.4: for an output as a table over the slew and the load, for an input over the slew, often depending on the state of the other pins. A flip-flop consumes internal power at every clock edge, even when its value does not change, because the clock switches its internal inverters and latches.
  • Leakage power. A transistor that is off still conducts a small current. The Liberty file gives the leakage of each cell, cell_leakage_power, and the leakage per input state (Section 5.4). Leakage flows as long as the supply is on, whatever the circuit does.

Switching and internal power together form the dynamic power, the leakage is the static power. The levers follow from the formula:

  • The supply voltage enters squared, but at a lower voltage, the cells are slower.
  • The clock frequency enters linearly. The energy per operation stays the same, though: a slower clock lowers the power, but not the energy of a computation. It saves energy only together with a lower supply voltage, which the longer period allows.
  • The activity drops when the clock of idle registers is switched off (clock gating, Section 7.7), when the operands of an unused operator are held constant (operand isolation), and when there are fewer glitches, the short pulses that unequal path delays produce at the output of a gate before it settles.
  • The capacitance drops with smaller cells, shorter wires, and fewer buffers, so area and power go together.
  • The leakage of an idle block disappears when switches cut off its supply (power gating). This needs isolation cells at the outputs of the block, a way to keep or restore its state, and a power-aware flow, which goes beyond this course. Libraries of advanced technologies also offer each cell with several threshold voltages, so that a path with slack can use slower cells that leak less.

7.6.1 Power Analysis with OpenSTA

OpenSTA computes the power of a netlist from the Liberty file, i.e., the pin capacitances, the internal power tables, and the leakage, and from the activity of every net. Without a simulation, it assumes by default that every input toggles in 10 % of the clock cycles, i.e., with an activity of 0.1 and a duty of 0.5, i.e., the input is 1 half of the time, and it propagates these activities through the logic. With a VCD file from a simulation of the netlist, read_vcd annotates the real activity of every net instead. The script syn/power.tcl does both:

syn/power.tcl
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Power analysis of a netlist <TOP>.nl.v in the current
# folder with OpenSTA and the constraints block.sdc. Usage:
# TOP=cg_reg sta -no_init -exit ../syn/power.tcl. VCD names a file
# with the activity of a simulation, whose testbench tb_<TOP> has
# the instance dut. Without VCD, every input except rst_ni toggles
# in 10 % of the clock cycles.
# CORNER selects the library corner (default typ_1p20V_25C).

set top $::env(TOP)
set corner typ_1p20V_25C
if {[info exists ::env(CORNER)]} { set corner $::env(CORNER) }
set lib $::env(PDK_ROOT)/ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell
read_liberty $lib/lib/sg13cmos5l_stdcell_$corner.lib
read_verilog $top.nl.v
link_design $top
read_sdc [file dirname [info script]]/block.sdc

# The activity of every net: from the simulation if there is one,
# otherwise the default activity at the inputs and a quiet reset
if {[info exists ::env(VCD)]} {
  read_vcd -scope tb_$top/dut $::env(VCD)
  report_activity_annotation
} else {
  set_power_activity -input_ports rst_ni -activity 0 -duty 1
}
report_power -digits 3

Without a simulation, the script keeps the reset inactive, since a reset that toggles in every tenth cycle would not be realistic. Here is the barrel shifter between two registers of Section 6.7, synthesized with the commands of that section:

cd /foss/designs/vlsi-design/content/sequential/code/bs_reg
TOP=bs_reg sta -no_init -exit ../../../synth_opt/code/syn/power.tcl

report_power sorts the cells into groups (Table 34): the flip-flops into Sequential, the logic into Combinational, the cells of the clock network, such as clock buffers and clock gates, into Clock, and the macros and pads into groups of their own, which are empty here. The switching power of a net counts for the cell that drives it.

The block consumes 1.72 mW, and 67 % of it in the flip-flops, 16.3 µW in each of them, although its inputs change in only one of ten cycles: the clock reaches every flip-flop in every cycle. Internal power dominates, and leakage is negligible at 25 °C. The group Clock is empty, because the netlist has no clock buffers before the layout, so a power analysis before clock tree synthesis misses the power of the clock tree.

The library of SG13CMOS5L is also characterized at 1.5 V. With CORNER=typ_1p50V_25C, the same netlist consumes 2.78 mW, 1.62 times as much, close to \((1.5/1.2)^2 = 1.56\), and the leakage rises from 0.19 to 0.56 µW. In return, the timing script of Section 6.7 reports a minimum period of 1.17 ns instead of 1.69 ns with CORNER=typ_1p50V_25C sta -no_init -exit syn/sta.tcl. The supply voltage trades speed against power.

7.7 Clock Gating

A register that keeps its value most of the time still consumes clock power in every cycle. SG13CMOS5L has no flip-flop with an enable (Section 3.4.3), so synthesis builds a register with an enable from a multiplexer in front of each flip-flop, which feeds back Q while the enable is low (Figure 28 (a)). Clock gating switches off the clock of the whole register instead, with one gate for all its flip-flops and without multiplexers (Figure 28 (b)).

A plain AND gate of clock and enable does not work (Figure 29). The enable comes from a register on the same clock, so it changes shortly after the rising edge, while the clock is high, and the AND gate passes the change at once. A rising enable produces a late clock edge, a falling one a short pulse, which clocks the register at the wrong time or violates the minimum pulse width of its flip-flops (Section 6.3).

An integrated clock gate (ICG) puts a latch, transparent while the clock is low, in front of the AND gate. The enable reaches the AND gate only during the low phase and stays stable while the clock is high, so the gated clock has only complete pulses. A flip-flop on the falling edge in place of the latch would give clean pulses as well, but the enable would have to arrive by the falling edge, i.e., within half a period. The latch accepts it until the rising edge. In SG13CMOS5L, the ICG is lgcp_1 with the pins GATE, CLK, and GCLK and an area of 27.2 µm², and its Liberty file marks it with clock_gating_integrated_cell : "latch_posedge". Its sibling slgcp_1 has an additional input SCE, which switches the clock on during the scan test (Section 9).

The clock passes through the ICG from CLK to GCLK, so STA times the gated flip-flops with the clock of the ICG. The path of the enable ends at the pin GATE, where the library defines a clock gating check, a setup and a hold check against the rising edge of CLK. Like the data input of a flip-flop, the enable must be stable shortly before the rising edge. The ICG also delays the clock of the gated flip-flops, which clock tree synthesis balances against the other flip-flops (Section 10).

Yosys inserts the ICGs with the pass clockgate, between synth and dfflibmap. It replaces each group of flip-flops that share a clock and an enable by one ICG and flip-flops without enable:

clockgate -pos sg13cmos5l_lgcp_1 GATE:CLK:GCLK -min_net_size 4

-pos names the ICG for flip-flops on the rising edge and its pins for the enable, the clock, and the gated clock. -min_net_size sets the smallest group that gets an ICG, since an ICG is clocked in every cycle and costs area and power of its own. LibreLane runs the same pass when SYNTH_CLOCKGATE_MIN_WIDTH is set, and it inserts ICGs when SYNTH_CLOCKGATE_POSEDGE_ICG names the cell, e.g., sg13cmos5l_lgcp_1/GATE/CLK/GCLK. The configuration of SG13CMOS5L sets neither and even excludes lgcp_1 and slgcp_1 from synthesis, so LibreLane gates no clocks unless a design configures it.
