Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: Make It Testable
  1. The second flip-flop of the synchronizer, rst_no, drives the reset inputs of all 21 flip-flops of bs_reg. A scan chain through all flip-flops passes through both synchronizer flip-flops, meta_q and rst_no.
  2. The chain has 23 flip-flops. The chain test reports 11 of 23 bits wrong, the scan test 32 patterns with 0 bits that differ.
  3. Whenever a 0 shifts into the flip-flop rst_no, its output resets all 21 flip-flops of bs_reg at once, and the bits they hold are lost. The scan test compares with a copy of the same netlist, which loses its bits in the same way, so all responses agree and the error stays hidden. With the expected values that an ATPG tool computes for an intact chain, the scan test would fail on every die, good or defective. Either way, the patterns are useless. This is why a test program starts with the chain test, and why ATPG tools check the reset rule before they generate patterns.
  4. A multiplexer in front of the reset of the registers (Figure 42):
  1. The reference solution:
reset/rtl/bs_reg_rs_tm.sv
// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Description: The barrel shifter between two registers behind a
// reset synchronizer (bs_reg_rs), with a test mode: during the scan
// test, the registers take their reset directly from the pin rst_ni.

`default_nettype none

module bs_reg_rs_tm #(
  parameter int unsigned WIDTH = 32  // power of two
) (
  input  logic                     clk_i,
  input  logic                     rst_ni,
  input  logic                     test_mode_i,  // 1 during the test
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0]         data_i,
  input  logic [$clog2(WIDTH)-1:0] shamt_i,
  input  logic [1:0]               mode_i,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0]         data_o
);

  logic rst_sync_n, rst_n;

  rst_sync u_rst_sync (
    .clk_i (clk_i),
    .rst_ni(rst_ni),
    .rst_no(rst_sync_n)
  );

  // In test mode, the tester controls the reset of the registers
  assign rst_n = test_mode_i ? rst_ni : rst_sync_n;

  bs_reg #(.WIDTH(WIDTH)) u_bs_reg (
    .clk_i  (clk_i),
    .rst_ni (rst_n),
    .data_i (data_i),
    .shamt_i(shamt_i),
    .mode_i (mode_i),
    .data_o (data_o)
  );

endmodule

`default_nettype wire

The chain test now reports 0 of 23 bits wrong. The fix costs one mux2_1 (18.1 µm²) in front of the 21 reset pins and one input. The total area changes by only 1.8 µm², from 2661.5 to 2663.3 µm², because ABC maps the barrel shifter slightly differently. In test mode, the multiplexer never selects rst_sync_n, so the path from the synchronizer to the registers is not tested. The two synchronizer flip-flops are still in the chain, and their inputs are tested at the capture.

9.7 Beyond Scan

Scan with stuck-at patterns is the backbone of the test of digital logic, but a complete test program contains more:

  • At-speed test. Stuck-at patterns can be shifted and captured slowly. A transition fault needs a launch and a capture exactly one functional clock period apart. In launch on capture (LOC), two capture pulses at the functional frequency follow the shift: the first launches the transition, the second captures it. In launch on shift (LOS), the last shift edge launches the transition, so scan_enable must fall within one functional period before the capture edge. The fast pulses come from the on-chip PLL, through a clock controller that the tester triggers.
  • Built-in self-test (BIST). A linear feedback shift register (LFSR) on the chip generates pseudo-random patterns, and a multiple-input signature register (MISR) compacts the responses into a signature, which is compared with the signature of the fault-free design at the end. The tester only starts the test and reads the result, which also works in the field, e.g., at every start of a car. A wrong response gives the fault-free signature, which is called aliasing, with a probability of only about \(2^{-n}\) for an \(n\)-bit MISR. Memories get a memory BIST: a controller writes and reads march patterns, sequences of writes and reads that walk up and down the addresses, and finds cells that are stuck, that disturb their neighbors, or that lose their data. The SRAM macros of SG13CMOS5L (Section 3.4.3) need such a controller, and a bypass, so that scan can test the logic around them.
  • Boundary scan (JTAG). The standard IEEE 1149.1 puts a scan cell at every pin of a chip and connects them into a chain, which the test access port (TAP) with the pins TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO, and optionally TRST controls. On a board, it tests the solder joints and the wires between the chips without probing them. The same port gives access to internal scan chains and to debug logic, e.g., of a processor. fault tap adds a TAP controller to a netlist with a scan chain.
  • Parametric tests and binning. Besides the logic, the test measures the quiescent current, the input thresholds and output drivers of the pads, and the maximum clock frequency, by which parts can be sorted into speed grades.
  • Diagnosis. When a die fails, its failing patterns and bits point to the faults that explain them, and the analysis of many failing dies shows the fab where its process creates defects.

The open-source DFT tools are moving as well. Difetto (Gaber 2026), a complete rewrite of Fault, adds the steps of this chapter to LibreLane as a plugin with three flows. The first is the LibreLane flow of Section 10 with extra steps: a Yosys plugin adds boundary-scan cells at the pins, replaces the flip-flops by scan flip-flops, and cuts them open for the ATPG, and OpenROAD stitches the chain after the detailed placement. The second generates the test vectors with Quaigh (Gouvine 2026), which starts with random vectors and then solves each remaining fault with a SAT solver on a miter, as sat_test.tcl does for single faults. The third checks the chain and applies the vectors with cocotb. In October 2026, Difetto is an alpha version, it is not part of the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS image, and it supports SG13G2 but not SG13CMOS5L, so this chapter uses OpenROAD and Fault.

9.8 Summary

  • Every manufactured die is tested, on the wafer and after packaging. The defect level \(1 - Y^{1-T}\) of the shipped parts depends on the yield and the fault coverage: 99 % coverage at 80 % yield leaves one defective part in 449.
  • The single stuck-at fault model fixes one net or pin at 0 or 1. Transition, bridging, and stuck-open faults and IDDQ testing cover other defects. Untestable faults sit in redundant logic. The test coverage leaves them out.
  • A test excites a fault, propagates the difference to an output, and justifies the required values from the inputs. ATPG tools start with random vectors and fault simulation and solve the rest with a deterministic search, today often with a SAT solver on a miter of the good and the faulty netlist.
  • Scan replaces every flip-flop by a scan flip-flop and connects them into chains. Shift, capture, and shift turn the test of a sequential circuit into a combinational one. A test of \(N\) patterns over chains of \(L\) flip-flops takes \((N + 1) L + N\) cycles. In the 8-bit bs_reg, scan insertion adds 12 % area. The 32 vectors of Fault detect every fault that its model can detect, but only 95.4 % of the detectable faults at the cell pins: coverage depends on the fault model.
  • Scan needs clocks and resets from pins, clock gates with a connected test enable, no latches, loops, or unknown values, one chain per clock domain, and hold-safe scan paths. A reset synchronizer needs a test-mode bypass, or the chain breaks while it shifts.
  • At-speed test, BIST for logic and memories, and boundary scan complete the test of a chip.

In Section 10, LibreLane takes the netlist through placement, clock tree synthesis, and routing to the layout. It inserts no scan chains, but the hold fixing and the equivalence check of this chapter return there.

10 The RTL-to-GDSII Flow with LibreLane

The netlists of the previous chapters exist only as text. To become a chip, every cell needs a place on the die, every net a wire in metal, and every clock a tree of buffers. The result must then pass the timing checks again, now with real wires, and checks that only a layout can fail: the design rules of the process and the comparison of the layout with the netlist. This chapter takes the barrel shifter between two registers of Section 6.7 through LibreLane (LibreLane Project 2026), the open-source RTL-to-GDSII flow of this course, from its RTL to a GDSII layout, one step at a time. It ends with the chip top level of the AMS chip template (Section 1.10), which puts such blocks into a padframe.

Note

All code of this chapter is available in the folder content/digital_flow/code of the course repository: the LibreLane configuration and the equivalence check of the barrel shifter in bs_reg/, a small design with a clock gate in cg_mix/, and one with a divided clock in div_mix/. All numbers in this chapter come from the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS image 2026.10 (LibreLane 3.1.0.dev3 with its OpenROAD 26Q1, Yosys 0.70, Magic 8.3.685, KLayout 0.30.12, Netgen 1.5.324, EQY 0.70) and SG13CMOS5L. The script scripts/check_digital_flow.sh reproduces all of them: run bash scripts/check_digital_flow.sh in the container from the root of the repository. It runs LibreLane seven times, at most two at a time, and takes about 25 minutes.

For the exercises, clone the course repository into your designs folder once, if you have not done so yet:

cd /foss/designs
git clone https://github.com/iic-jku/vlsi-design.git

In every new terminal, define the path of the typical-corner library:

LIB=$PDK_ROOT/ihp-sg13cmos5l/libs.ref/sg13cmos5l_stdcell/lib
LIB=$LIB/sg13cmos5l_stdcell_typ_1p20V_25C.lib

10.1 Learning Objectives

After this chapter, you will be able to:

  • run LibreLane on a block and find the results of every step in its run folder
  • plan a floorplan: the size of the core, the rows, the power grid, and the pins
  • explain what placement, buffering, clock tree synthesis, timing repair, and routing do to a netlist
  • read the signoff results: timing in all corners, IR drop, DRC, LVS, and the equivalence of the final netlist with the RTL
  • explain why the estimates before routing are optimistic, and close timing with the right setting
  • describe how a block becomes part of a chip with a padframe

10.2 LibreLane

LibreLane is a Python program that runs the tools of the flow one after the other: Verilator for the lint, Yosys for the synthesis, OpenROAD for floorplan, placement, clock tree, and routing, OpenRCX for the extraction, OpenSTA for the timing, Magic and KLayout for the layout and its design rules, and Netgen for the comparison of the layout with the netlist. Each step reads the state of the design that the previous step left, i.e., the netlist and the layout database, runs one tool, and writes the new state. Checkers between the steps stop the flow on errors, e.g., on unmapped cells, on wires that break a design rule, or on a failed comparison. A flow is a list of steps. The Classic flow of Figure 43 hardens a block from RTL to GDSII into a macro, a finished layout that a parent design places like a large cell, and the Chip flow of Section 10.8 adds the padframe.

A YAML file configures the run: the name of the top module, the RTL files, the clock, the constraints, the floorplan, and the corners. Everything it does not set comes from the defaults of LibreLane and of the PDK, which libs.tech/librelane/ of SG13CMOS5L holds. The configuration of bs_reg uses the SDC file of Section 6.6 for placement, routing, and signoff, a core with 50 % utilization, and the supply nets VDD and VSS of the AMS chip template. The corners come from the PDK: the typical, slow, and fast corners of Section 5.6 for the nominal supply of 1.2 V, with the typical one as the default corner, which the timing reports between the steps use. LibreLane names each corner after the corner of the wires and the corner of the library, e.g., nom_typ_1p20V_25C for nominal wires and the typical library at 1.2 V and 25 °C:

bs_reg/config.yaml
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: LibreLane configuration of the barrel shifter between
# two registers (bs_reg, 32 bits) of chapter 6. Usage, in this folder:
#   librelane config.yaml --pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l --pdk-root $PDK_ROOT \
#     --manual-pdk --run-tag base
# The run lands in runs/base, its results in runs/base/final.

meta:
  version: 3
  flow: Classic

DESIGN_NAME: bs_reg
VERILOG_FILES:
  - dir::../../../verification/code/barrel_shift/rtl/barrel_shift.sv
  - dir::../../../sequential/code/bs_reg/rtl/bs_reg.sv

# The clock and the constraints of chapter 6
CLOCK_PORT: clk_i
CLOCK_PERIOD: 4.0
PNR_SDC_FILE: dir::../../../sequential/code/bs_reg/syn/bs_reg.sdc
SIGNOFF_SDC_FILE: dir::../../../sequential/code/bs_reg/syn/bs_reg.sdc

# Floorplan: the core takes the cells at the target utilization
FP_SIZING: relative
FP_CORE_UTIL: 50
PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT: 60

# The supply nets, named as in the AMS chip template
VDD_NETS: [VDD]
GND_NETS: [VSS]

# The library; its corners come from the PDK: typical, slow, and fast
# at 1.2 V, with the typical one as the default corner
STD_CELL_LIBRARY: sg13cmos5l_stdcell

The run takes about six minutes. LibreLane writes each step into its own numbered folder of the run folder runs/base/, e.g., 06-yosys-synthesis/ or 35-openroad-cts/, with the log of the tool, its reports, the exact commands in COMMANDS, and the state it hands on. The folder final/ collects the results: the layout as GDSII (gds/), as DEF (Design Exchange Format, def/), and as OpenROAD database (odb/), the LEF abstract of the macro for a parent design (Section 5.3, lef/), the netlist without and with supply connections (nl/, pnl/), the extracted parasitics as SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format, spef/), the delays for a gate-level simulation per corner as SDF (Section 4.10.2, sdf/), a timing model of the macro (lib/), the SPICE netlist extracted from the layout (spice/), and all metrics of the run in metrics.json.

10.3 Floorplan

The die is the rectangle of the macro, the core the area inside it where the cells stand. The margins between them hold the pins and, in a chip, a ring of supply wires. With FP_SIZING: relative, LibreLane derives the core from the area of the synthesized cells: FP_CORE_UTIL: 50 makes the core twice as large as the cells, and the core is square unless an aspect ratio is set. The free half is not wasted. Placement adds buffers, clock tree synthesis adds a tree, timing repair enlarges cells, and the router needs free tracks above the cells. The other way is FP_SIZING: absolute with a fixed DIE_AREA, as in the counter of the AMS chip template.

The core is divided into rows of the height of a cell, 3.78 µm in SG13CMOS5L, made of sites of 0.48 µm width (Section 5.3). Every cell is a whole number of sites wide. Every second row is flipped, so that two neighboring rows share their supply rail. Many libraries need tap cells in every row, which tie the wells and the substrate to the supplies. The cells of SG13CMOS5L contain these ties themselves, so the PDK sets FP_TAPCELL_DIST to 0, and the flow inserts none.

The power distribution network (PDN) brings VDD and VSS to every row (Figure 44). Metal1 rails run along the rows, where the cells connect to them. Vertical straps on Metal4, 1 µm wide every 50 µm, connect to the rails through stacks of vias, and horizontal straps on TopMetal1, 2 µm wide every 50 µm, connect to the Metal4 straps. The straps of both layers form the supply pins of the macro, to which the parent connects its own grid. The pins of the signals sit on the edges of the die, on Metal3 on the left and right and on Metal2 at the top and bottom, the layers whose preferred direction leads into the core. The IO placer orders them to keep the wires short, or follows a pin order file.

TipExercise: Plan the Floorplan

All commands start in the folder content/digital_flow/code/bs_reg. Start the run first, it takes about six minutes:

librelane config.yaml --pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l --pdk-root $PDK_ROOT \
  --manual-pdk --run-tag base

  1. Sketch the floorplan of bs_reg with the core, the rows, the straps, and the pins, and add the numbers: the synthesis report runs/base/06-yosys-synthesis/reports/stat.rpt gives the area of the synthesized cells. Compute the core for 50 % utilization, its edge for a square core, and the number of rows and sites that fit.

  2. Compare with the layout: runs/base/final/def/bs_reg.def holds the die (DIEAREA) and one ROW statement per row, in database units of 1 nm. How large are the die and the core, and how wide are the margins? Which utilization and cell area does runs/base/final/metrics.json report for the finished layout (design__instance__utilization, design__instance__area__stdcell), and how much area did the steps after the synthesis add?

  3. Run the flow again with a denser core and a higher density limit for the placement (PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT, Section 10.4):

    librelane config.yaml --pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l --pdk-root $PDK_ROOT \
  --manual-pdk --run-tag util75 \
  -c FP_CORE_UTIL=75 -c PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT=85

    How do the utilization, the wire length (route__wirelength), the number of iterations of the detailed router (Section 10.6, route__drc_errors__iter:N), and the worst setup slack in the typical corner change? Is a smaller core worth it here?

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: Plan the Floorplan
  1. The synthesized cells take 13,008.1 µm², so the core needs 26,016 µm², an edge of 161.3 µm. That fits 42 rows of 3.78 µm (158.76 µm) and 336 sites of 0.48 µm (161.28 µm). Metal1 rails run along the rows. Over the 161 µm of the core, the Metal4 straps every 50 µm make 4 for VDD and 3 for VSS, alternating, and TopMetal1 has 3 pairs. The pins sit on all four edges.
  2. The rows fill 161.28 × 158.76 µm, 25,604.8 µm², with 42 rows of 336 sites. The die is 172.82 × 191.54 µm: the computed edge of 161.30 µm plus margins of 12 sites (5.76 µm) left and right and of 4 rows (15.12 µm) at the bottom and top. Of the computed square, 0.02 µm at the right and 2.54 µm at the top do not fill a whole site or row and stay empty. The finished layout reports 58.7 % utilization, 15,023.2 µm² of cells, because placement, clock tree synthesis, and timing repair added 2015 µm² of buffers and larger cells.
  3. With 75 %, the core shrinks to 16,903 µm², and the finished layout fills 89.2 % of it. The detailed router starts with 1139 instead of 683 violations and needs 6 instead of 4 iterations, the wire length grows from 40,693 to 45,974 µm, and the worst setup slack in the typical corner drops from 1.075 to 0.997 ns. The core is 34 % smaller, but harder to route and slower. For a macro that the parent places in a fixed slot, the margin is worth more.

10.4 Placement

Global placement spreads the cells over the core so that the total wire length is short and no region is denser than PL_TARGET_DENSITY_PCT. OpenROAD treats the cells like charges that repel each other, while the nets pull connected cells together, and the result still allows overlaps. After it, OpenROAD can estimate the wires for STA: it approximates each net by a tree through its pins and multiplies the length by a resistance and a capacitance per micron. LibreLane takes both from the technology LEF, averaged over the routing layers Metal2 to TopMetal1: 0.389 Ω/µm and 0.097 fF/µm, against 0.515 Ω/µm and 0.093 fF/µm for Metal2 alone.

Then the repair of the design fixes every net that breaks a limit of the library or the constraints: the maximum slew, the maximum capacitance, and the maximum fanout. The SDC of bs_reg sets no fanout limit, so the default of the Liberty file applies, 8 loads (default_max_fanout). A design without an SDC file of its own gets the SDC of LibreLane, which sets the 10 loads of the PDK (MAX_FANOUT_CONSTRAINT). For bs_reg, OpenROAD first puts a buf_1 behind each of the 40 inputs and in front of each of the 32 outputs, which separates the inside of the macro from its surroundings. It then finds 5 nets with too slow a slew and 30 nets with more than 8 loads, and inserts 142 more buffers into them. Synthesis did not do this: LibreLane’s default synthesis strategy, AREA 0, lets ABC insert buffers only when SYNTH_ABC_BUFFERING is set, which is off by default, so its netlist has no buffers at all (Section 5.7). Detailed placement finally moves every cell onto a site of a row, without overlaps.

10.5 Clock Tree Synthesis

Until now, the timing analyses of our designs assumed an ideal clock that reaches every flip-flop at the same moment (Section 6.6). In reality, one clock pin cannot drive dozens of flip-flops spread over the core. Clock tree synthesis (CTS) builds a tree of buffers from the clock pin to every flip-flop, so that the clock edge reaches all of them after about the same delay, the latency, with a small difference, the skew. TritonCTS, the CTS of OpenROAD, builds an H-tree: it divides the region of the flip-flops recursively into halves, connects the halves with branches of equal length, and places buffers along the tree that drive the branches and the flip-flops. It chooses from the clock buffers that the PDK lists, buf_8 down to buf_1, with buf_8 at the root. From now on, STA uses the propagated clock, i.e., the real arrival time of the clock at each flip-flop.

Skew moves time from one check to the other (Section 6.10): a capturing flip-flop whose clock arrives late gains setup time and loses hold time. After CTS, OpenROAD therefore repairs the timing with the real clock: it enlarges cells and adds buffers on paths that violate setup, and it inserts delay cells, dlygate4sd1_1 to dlygate4sd3_1, into paths that violate hold, up to the margins PL_RESIZER_SETUP_SLACK_MARGIN and PL_RESIZER_HOLD_SLACK_MARGIN (0.05 and 0.1 ns by default). The candidates for hold violations are short paths, in which one flip-flop drives the next directly, as in the scan chains of Section 9.

A clock gate (Section 7.7) sits inside the clock tree, and the flip-flops behind it see its delay on top of the tree. TritonCTS balances this extra delay. The design cg_mix has two 16-bit registers on one clock, one of them behind an lgcp_1. CTS builds one tree behind the clock gate and one for the ungated register, reports that it balances the latency of the clock, and inserts three buf_8 as delay buffers in front of the tree of the ungated register. In the typical corner, all 32 flip-flops then see the rising clock edge between 0.381 and 0.440 ns after the clock pin.

A divided clock (Section 3.4.2) gets no such help. In div_mix, a flip-flop divides clk_i by two, and a 16-bit register on the divided clock takes over the value of a register on clk_i. Its SDC file defines the divided clock with create_generated_clock (Section 6.8). CTS finds two clock nets, clk_i and the output div_q of the divider, and builds a tree for each without balancing them against each other. The flip-flops behind the divider therefore see the clock later, by the clock-to-output delay of the divider and the delay of the second tree, and after CTS all 16 paths from clk_i into the divided clock violate hold, by up to 0.25 ns in the typical corner. The timing repair fixes them with 32 delay cells, two in front of each flip-flop. A clock enable on clk_i needs neither the second tree nor the delay cells.

TipExercise: Follow the Clock and the Reset

All commands start in the folder content/digital_flow/code/bs_reg and use the run base of the previous exercise.

  1. Sketch the clock tree of bs_reg from the log of CTS, runs/base/35-openroad-cts/openroad-cts.log: how many flip-flops does it drive, how many buffers did it create, how many buffers are in each clock path, and how many flip-flops does each last buffer drive? What are the dummy loads that CTS reports?

  2. How large is the skew? The worst skew of each corner is in runs/base/final/metrics.json (clock__skew__worst_setup__corner:...). Which output drives the only fanout violation of the run (runs/base/55-openroad-stapostpnr/nom_typ_1p20V_25C/checks.rpt), and why did the repair of the design not fix it?

  3. The reset input rst_ni drives the RESET_B pins of all flip-flops. Follow it in the final netlist runs/base/final/nl/bs_reg.nl.v: how many buffers lie between rst_ni and a flip-flop at most, and how many RESET_B pins does one buffer drive at most? How large is the worst recovery slack in the typical and the slow corner? The path that starts at rst_ni in the file max.rpt of each corner shows it.

  4. No path needed a hold repair. Ask for a larger hold margin and run again:

    librelane config.yaml --pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l --pdk-root $PDK_ROOT \
  --manual-pdk --run-tag hold05 \
  -c PL_RESIZER_HOLD_SLACK_MARGIN=0.5

    Which of the delay cells did the flow choose, how many did it insert, and how much area do they cost? Is the margin reached?

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: Follow the Clock and the Reset
  1. The clock net clk_i has 71 sinks. CTS builds an H-tree with 17 buf_8: one at the root, which drives 16 leaf buffers, and each leaf drives 4 or 5 flip-flops (9 × 4 + 7 × 5 = 71). Every clock path has exactly 2 buffers. The 9 leaves with only 4 flip-flops get a dummy load, an inv_1 whose output stays open, so that all 16 leaves carry about the same load and the same delay. Together they make the 80 sinks that the log reports.
  2. The worst setup skew is 0.118 ns in the typical corner, 0.124 ns in the slow and 0.116 ns in the fast one. The fanout violation belongs to the root buffer clkbuf_0_clk_i, which drives 16 leaves against a limit of 8. The repair of the design ran before CTS and skips clock nets anyway, and CTS groups the sinks by the load its buffers can drive, not by the fanout limit.
  3. The repair of the design turned the reset net into a tree of 13 buf_1, the input buffer included, and the RESET_B pins hang on 12 of its nets, with 2 to 8 pins each. At most five buffers lie between rst_ni and a flip-flop. In Section 6.7, one buf_2 drove all 71 pins with a slew of 0.87 ns. The tree splits this load, at the price of more delay, which the recovery check easily allows: its worst slack is 1.912 ns in the typical and 1.356 ns in the slow corner.
  4. The flow inserts 131 dlygate4sd3_1, the delay cell with the largest delay, and the area of the cells grows by 14 %, from 15,023.2 to 17,162.4 µm². The resizer still warns that it cannot repair all hold checks within the margin: it reaches only 0.22 ns on its estimates, and at signoff the fast corner has 0.268 ns, far below the 0.5 ns asked for. Hold margin costs area, so the default asks for 0.1 ns only.

10.6 Routing

Global routing divides the die into a grid of tiles, assigns each net a path through the tiles and a layer, and counts the demand of each tile against its tracks. A tile with more demand than tracks is congested, and the router detours nets around it. For bs_reg, the global router uses 44 % of the tracks of Metal2 and 39 % of Metal3, 28 % of all tracks, without overflow, i.e., no tile is congested. STA can now use the global routes instead of the estimates of the placement. LibreLane can also repair the timing once more on them, but this step (RUN_POST_GRT_RESIZER_TIMING) is off by default. Global routing also checks the antenna rule: while a wire is being manufactured, it collects charge, and a long wire that ends at a gate can damage the gate oxide before the upper metal connects it to a diffusion that drains the charge. The fix is a jumper to a higher layer or a diode cell, antennanp in SG13CMOS5L, next to the gate. bs_reg has no violation and needs no diode.

Detailed routing with TritonRoute draws every wire on the tracks of its layer, with the widths, spacings, and vias that the design rules demand. It starts from a first solution with violations and repairs them in iterations: for bs_reg, 683 violations after the first iteration, then 355 and 296, and none after the fourth. The routed wires are 40,693 µm long, and the longest net 436 µm.

After routing, fill insertion closes the gaps in the rows with filler cells, which continue the wells and the rails, and with decoupling capacitors (Section 5.3): 634 decap_8 and 151 decap_4, which hold charge between VDD and VSS where cells switch, and 255 fill_2 and 280 fill_1 in the gaps that are too small for them. Figure 45 shows the finished layout.

10.7 Signoff

Only now are the wires known. Parasitic extraction with OpenRCX computes the resistance of every wire and its capacitance to ground and to its neighbors from the routed layout and the rules of the PDK, and writes them as SPEF. STA reads the SPEF instead of the estimates, and it writes SDF files with the delays of every cell and every wire, which a gate-level simulation can back-annotate (Section 4.10). The signoff STA checks setup and hold in every corner, the slow corner for setup and the fast one for hold in particular, and LibreLane collects the results in 55-openroad-stapostpnr/summary.rpt.

Figure 46 follows the worst setup slack through the run. The synthesized netlist misses the 4 ns clock, because ABC left the high-fanout nets unbuffered. After the repair of the design and CTS, the slack is positive, and the timing repair adds to it. Then the slack shrinks again, from 1.45 ns after the timing repair to 1.08 ns: the global routes cost 0.11 ns, and the extracted wires another 0.26 ns. The estimates before routing are optimistic: real wires take detours and change layers through vias, and the extraction counts the capacitance between neighboring wires, which the estimate per micron does not.

Besides timing, the signoff checks the layout itself:

  • IR drop. OpenROAD computes the voltage drop in the power grid for the estimated currents of the cells. The worst drop on VDD in bs_reg is 1.33 mV, 0.11 % of the 1.2 V supply, and VSS rises by at most 1.99 mV.
  • DRC. Magic and KLayout check the GDSII against the design rules of the PDK, with 0 violations each for bs_reg. KLayout also compares the GDSII files that Magic and KLayout stream out (an XOR, 0 differences).
  • LVS. Magic extracts a netlist from the layout, and Netgen compares it with the netlist with supply connections (pnl/): “Circuits match uniquely”. In the flow, the cells are abstracts, boxes with their pins and nothing inside, so the comparison covers the connections between the cells and not the transistors inside them. The AMS chip template can also run a full LVS of the GDSII with KLayout (make klayout-lvs).
  • Antenna. A second antenna check on the routed layout, with 0 violations.

One more check proves that the netlist still does what the RTL describes. The layout flow changed it: buffers, a clock tree, resized cells, and delay cells. LibreLane’s own equivalence step prepares the cell models only for sky130, so we run EQY ourselves on the final netlist, with the setup of Section 5.8. Flattening the RTL keeps the net names of the submodule u_shift as second names of the nets of bs_reg, which would confuse the matching, so both sides hide the hierarchical names:

bs_reg/lec.eqy
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Simon Dorrer
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
# Description: Equivalence check of bs_reg: its RTL (gold) against the
# final netlist of the LibreLane run in runs/base (gate). Run in this
# folder with stdcell.lib linked to the typical library of SG13CMOS5L:
# eqy -d lec_eqy lec.eqy

[gold]
plugin -i slang
read_slang --top bs_reg \
  ../../../verification/code/barrel_shift/rtl/barrel_shift.sv \
  ../../../sequential/code/bs_reg/rtl/bs_reg.sv
hierarchy -check -top bs_reg
proc
flatten -noscopeinfo
# Flattening keeps the net names of the submodule as second names
rename -hide w:*.*

[gate]
# The cell functions come from the Liberty file
read_liberty -ignore_miss_func stdcell.lib
read_verilog runs/base/final/nl/bs_reg.nl.v
hierarchy -check -top bs_reg
flatten -noscopeinfo
# Fails if a cell had no model and stayed a black box
select -assert-none t:sg13cmos5l_*
rename -hide w:*.*

[strategy sby]
use sby
engine abc pdr
TipExercise: Close the Timing

All commands start in the folder content/digital_flow/code/bs_reg and use the run base of the first exercise.

  1. Sketch the worst path of the failing corner. Open runs/base/55-openroad-stapostpnr/summary.rpt: which corner fails, by how much, and at how many endpoints? Then draw the worst path of that corner from the file max.rpt in the folder of the corner: where does it start, through which cells does it run, and where does it end?

  2. The timing repair after CTS worked on all corners. Read its log, runs/base/37-openroad-resizertimingpostcts/openroad-resizertimingpostcts.log: from which worst slack did it start, and which did it reach? How much slack did the slow corner lose between the repair and signoff, compared with the typical corner in Figure 46?

  3. Try a delay-oriented synthesis first, -c SYNTH_STRATEGY="DELAY 4" with --run-tag delay4. What happens to the slack in the slow corner and to the area of the cells (design__instance__area__stdcell)?

  4. Ask the repair for a setup margin of 0.6 ns, -c PL_RESIZER_SETUP_SLACK_MARGIN=0.6 with --run-tag margin. Why this value? Do all corners pass now, and at which cost in area?

  5. The resizer changed the netlist. Prove that the final netlist of runs/base still implements the RTL:

    ln -sf $LIB stdcell.lib
eqy -f -d lec_eqy lec.eqy

    What does EQY report? Then replace the first sg13cmos5l_a21oi_1 in the file by sg13cmos5l_o21ai_1 in a copy of the netlist, point read_verilog in a copy of lec.eqy to it, and check again.

Before continuing, please finish the previous exercise. Once you are done, compare with the solution below.

TipSolution: Close the Timing
  1. The slow corner fails with a worst setup slack of -0.586 ns at 31 endpoints, with a total of -6.98 ns, while the typical corner has 1.075 ns and the fast corner 2.072 ns. Hold passes everywhere, with 0.204 ns in the fast corner. The worst path starts at _1537_, the flip-flop of shamt_q[1], and ends at the input of a flip-flop of out_q. Of the 3.59 ns from the output of the first flip-flop to the input of the second, 1.83 ns go into six buffers of the repair of the design: two behind the flip-flop, whose output drove 36 loads before the repair, and a chain of four behind an XNOR gate, whose output drove 53. The rest goes into the XNOR gate, two multiplexers, and four other gates.
  2. The repair started at -0.725 ns, the worst slack over all corners, i.e., in the slow corner, resized 8 cells, removed one buffer, and reached +0.031 ns on its estimates, below its margin of 0.05 ns, so it reported that it could not repair all violations. After routing, the slow corner ends at -0.586 ns, so it lost 0.62 ns on the way to signoff, against 0.38 ns in the typical corner. The estimates before routing are optimistic, and the slow corner suffers most, because its weaker cells turn the same extra capacitance into more delay.
  3. With DELAY 4, the slow corner improves only to -0.542 ns, while the area of the cells grows by 12 % to 16,852.1 µm². The synthesis was not the problem: the repair reached 0.088 ns on its estimates, above its margin, and the wires again took 0.63 ns.
  4. The margin covers the loss of about 0.6 ns that the slow corner showed in the second step. With it, all corners pass: 0.048 ns in the slow corner, 1.512 ns in the typical corner. The cells take 15,170.2 µm², only 1 % more than in base. The right knob depends on the mechanism: here the estimate before routing was the problem, not the logic.
  5. EQY proves the designs equivalent in 32 partitions, one per output bit, in less than half a minute. With the replaced cell, it fails the partitions of two output bits, data_o[1] and data_o[17]. The equivalence check belongs after every step that changes the netlist, and the layout flow changes it a lot.

10.8 Chip Assembly

A macro is not yet a chip. The chip top level of the AMS chip template (Section 1.10) places the macros into a core and surrounds it with a padframe: a ring of IO cells, each with its bondpad, which drive the signals off the chip, protect the inputs against electrostatic discharge, and bring in the supplies (Figure 47). It runs LibreLane’s Chip flow, the Classic flow with additional steps: one builds the padframe, one draws the seal ring, a wall of all metal and via layers along the edge of the die that stops cracks from the sawing and keeps moisture out, and two insert the fill and check its density. In its configuration, flow/librelane/config.yaml of the template:

  • The die is 1.6 × 1.6 mm, with the core from 365 to 1235 µm in both directions, and the clock is 20 ns.
  • Four lists, PAD_WEST, PAD_NORTH, PAD_SOUTH, and PAD_EAST, name the 32 pad instances of the RTL in the order in which they line up on each side: inputs, outputs, bidirectional pads with the tri-state drivers of Section 3.4.4, analog pads, and the supply pads for the core (VDD, VSS, 1.5 V) and for the IO cells (IOVDD, IOVSS, 3.3 V).
  • The timing is signed off for both core supplies of the PDK, in the typical, slow, and fast corners at 1.2 V and at 1.5 V, with the typical corner at 1.5 V as the default.
  • The block MACROS lists each macro with its GDSII and LEF and, where they exist, its netlists, parasitics, and timing models per corner, and places its instances at fixed positions and orientations. PDN_MACRO_CONNECTIONS connects the two supply pairs of the SRAM to the grid of the core, and the other macros get their supplies through their power pins in the RTL.
  • A core ring of 15 µm wide supply wires surrounds the core and connects to the supply pads (PDN_CORE_RING_CONNECT_TO_PADS).
  • A non-default routing rule gives the analog nets wires of 0.5 µm width and spacing on Metal1 to Metal4, and the resizer must not touch them.

The template switches off the fill step of the flow. After the run, it adds the chip logo and then the fill, which brings the density of the active area and of every metal layer into the window that manufacturing demands, e.g., 35 to 60 % on Metal1 to Metal4, checks the whole chip with the DRC of Magic (KLayout runs its DRC and LVS with make klayout-drc and make klayout-lvs), and draws the bonding diagram for the package. Section 11 builds a chip this way.

10.9 Summary

  • LibreLane runs the flow as a list of steps, each with its own folder of logs and reports in the run folder, and collects GDSII, LEF, netlists, SPEF, SDF, and metrics in final/. A YAML file sets what the defaults of LibreLane and the PDK do not.
  • The floorplan sizes the core from the cell area and a utilization, divides it into rows of 3.78 µm, and builds the power grid from Metal1 rails and Metal4 and TopMetal1 straps.
  • Placement spreads the cells and buffers every net beyond the limits of slew, capacitance, and fanout, e.g., the reset net. CTS builds an H-tree of buf_8 with a small skew and balances clock gates, but not divided clocks. The timing repair fixes setup and hold with the propagated clock.
  • Routing assigns and draws every wire, repairs antenna violations, and fill insertion adds decaps and fillers.
  • Signoff extracts the wires and checks the timing in all corners, the IR drop, the design rules, and the layout against the netlist. EQY then proves the final netlist equivalent to the RTL. The estimates before routing are optimistic, so the repair needs a margin, and in bs_reg the slow corner passes with a setup margin of 0.6 ns.
  • The chip top level of the AMS chip template runs LibreLane’s Chip flow, which places the macros in a core inside a padframe of IO cells and bondpads and draws the seal ring.

In Section 11, these steps build a complete chip with the AMS chip template.

11 Capstone Project: A Small RISC-V SoC

This chapter will be released later in the semester.

12 Appendix: Exam Questions

This appendix collects possible questions for the written exam (Section 1.5), grouped by the chapters of the course. The last two sections hold calculation problems and problems in which you read, write, or fix code, constraints, and reports. The exam is based on these questions, partly with other numbers, circuits, or code.

The exam is written and allows no technical aids. Most questions therefore ask for an explanation, often with a sketch, and the calculations need only simple arithmetic, with every value and constant given in the question. If you have worked through the exercises of the chapters, you have practiced most of what these questions ask. The practical work with the tools is assessed in the project (Section 11).

12.1 Introduction

  1. Compare the ASIC implementation styles FPGA, gate array, standard-cell IC, and full-custom IC by the masks they need, the design effort, the trade-off between non-recurring engineering cost and unit cost, and their typical use. Which style does this course use, and what does the designer describe in it?

  2. Draw the RTL-to-GDSII flow from the RTL to the tapeout, and explain each step in one sentence. Where does a design iteration go back to when the timing is not met?

12.2 Hardware Description with SystemVerilog

  1. How does a hardware description differ from a program for a microcontroller? Use a for loop to explain computing in time and computing in space, and what happens to the run time and the area when the loop bound grows.

  2. How does SystemVerilog extend and truncate the operands of an expression? Give an example in which a carry is lost without a warning and one in which a comparison with a constant is always false. How do you keep the carry, and what happens when signed and unsigned operands are mixed?

  3. Explain the difference between the blocking assignment = and the non-blocking assignment <=. What happens when two registers that should swap their values are written with blocking assignments in one always_ff block, and what happens when the two blocking assignments sit in two separate always_ff blocks? State the golden rules of processes.

  4. Explain the two-process style in SystemVerilog. What belongs in the always_ff block and what in the always_comb block, what do the suffixes _d and _q stand for, and which advantages does the style have?

  5. When does a combinational block infer a latch, and why is an unintended latch almost always a bug in a synchronous design? How does a default assignment prevent it, and what do Verilator and Yosys report for a latch in always_comb? Is a register that keeps its value while its clock enable is low a latch?

  6. What is the difference between a Moore and a Mealy FSM? A controller raises done_o for one clock cycle when a job ends. Compare a Moore and a Mealy version by the number of states, the cycle in which done_o is high, and the risks of the output.

  7. What makes a testbench self-checking? Why does a testbench drive the inputs and check the outputs on the falling clock edge? How must a failing check end an Icarus Verilog simulation, and what must the runner of a cocotb testbench do, so that a script sees the failure?

12.3 Modeling Guidelines for Synthesizable RTL

  1. Why must the simulation of the RTL agree with that of the netlist, and what are the typical causes of a mismatch? What can a gate-level simulation see that a logic equivalence check cannot, and the other way round?

  2. What do X-optimism and X-pessimism mean? How do an if, a case whose default assigns 'x, and the conditional operator ?: treat an unknown select in Icarus Verilog, and how does an AND gate treat an unknown input? Why does Verilator show no x at all, and why should RTL never assign 'x?

  3. Which registers need a reset, and which may stay without one? Why can the missing reset of an FSM stay invisible in an RTL simulation, and which simulations reveal it?

  4. Name four habits from FPGA design that break on an ASIC, and what you use instead. Why in particular is a register output that clocks other registers a problem, and how does a clock enable avoid it?

  5. An exclusive counter can be built as a binary counter with a decoder, as a one-hot ring, or as a Johnson counter with a decoder. Compare the three architectures by area, speed, glitches at the outputs, and robustness against a wrong state. Does the coding style, e.g., a for loop instead of a concatenation for the ring, change the netlist?

12.4 Functional Verification with cocotb

  1. Distinguish verification, test, and validation. What does each of them ask, and when does it happen? What is the fundamental limit of simulation?

  2. Draw a testbench with generator, driver, monitor, reference model, scoreboard, and coverage collector, and explain each block. Why is the reference model written from the specification and not from the RTL, and which blocks merge for a combinational design?

  3. Compare directed, exhaustive, and constrained-random stimuli, and explain how you reproduce a random test that failed. Why can an exhaustive test of the 8-bit instance of a parameterized barrel shifter miss a bug of its 32-bit instance?

  4. Name the four kinds of code coverage that Verilator measures. What is functional coverage, and how can a test reach 100 % line, branch, and expression coverage while it misses most of the functional bins? What does no kind of coverage measure?

  5. What is the difference between an immediate and a concurrent assertion? Explain |->, |=>, disable iff, and $stable(). Why are the concurrent assertions of the course kept in a separate checker attached with bind?

  6. What is mutation testing? Explain killed, surviving, and equivalent mutants, and the two possible reasons why a mutant survives.

  7. What does an SDF file hold, and what does back-annotation mean? Why can a timing simulation with Icarus Verilog pass at clock periods for which static timing analysis reports violations, and which of the two do you trust for the tapeout?

12.5 Logic Synthesis and the Standard-Cell Library

  1. Describe the four steps of logic synthesis from the RTL to a netlist of standard cells. Which Yosys commands perform them?

  2. What is a standard cell? Explain rows, sites, shared supply rails, and the drive strength of a cell, and name the views of a standard-cell library with the steps of the flow that read them.

  3. What information does a Liberty file hold for a cell? Explain a timing arc and its timing sense, with an example of a positive unate, a negative unate, and a non-unate arc. Between which points of the waveforms are a delay and a slew measured?

  4. What is the propagation delay of a cell, and what does it depend on? How does the nonlinear delay model store it, how does a timing tool compute the delay between the table entries, and why is the delay of a path computed stage by stage?

  5. What is a wire-load model, from what does it estimate the capacitance of a wire, and when is it used? Which wire capacitances do the pre-layout timing analyses of this book include?

  6. What are process, voltage, and temperature corners? Which corner usually limits the setup check and which the hold check, and why does the signoff check both in all corners?

  7. What does a logic equivalence check prove, and why does a netlist need one, although synthesis produced it from the RTL? Explain gold, gate, the matching of registers, cut points, and cones, and name two cases in which the check fails falsely.

  8. An equivalence check fails in one partition. How do you decide whether the netlist has a bug or the check failed falsely, and why should a check that passes also be shown to fail on a broken netlist?

12.6 Sequential Elements and Static Timing Analysis

  1. What are the setup time and the hold time of a flip-flop, and what can happen when the data changes inside the window that they form? Name the other timing parameters of a flip-flop with an asynchronous reset, and explain what a negative hold time means.

  2. Draw a path between two registers with the clock tree that drives both. What are clock latency, clock skew, clock uncertainty, and jitter?

  3. Write the setup and the hold condition of a register-to-register path, including skew and uncertainty, and define the slack of each check. Describe a setup and a hold violation. Why does a lower clock frequency fix a setup violation but not a hold violation?

  4. Describe static timing analysis in one sentence. What are startpoints, endpoints, and the four kinds of timing paths, and what are WNS and TNS? What can static timing analysis not check?

  5. A register output clocks other registers. What does STA do with the paths behind it if the constraints do not mention this clock, and how does check_setup reveal it? Which constraint fixes the analysis, and which paths does the tool time once it knows the generated clock?

  6. What are false paths and multicycle paths? Why does a multicycle path with 2 cycles for setup also need an exception of 1 cycle for hold? Why should a design have few timing exceptions?

  7. How are setup and hold violations fixed, and on which paths do hold violations typically appear? The capturing flip-flop of a shift register of two flip-flops gets its clock through four buffers, and the analysis uses no clock uncertainty. Why can its hold check be worst in the slow corner?

12.7 Synthesis Optimizations and Low-Power Design

  1. Explain the generate and the propagate signal of an adder, its carry recursion, and the prefix operator. Compare the ripple-carry, Brent-Kung, and Kogge-Stone adders by the number of levels and of prefix operators, and draw the prefix graph of an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder.

  2. A prefix adder written with + comes out of synthesis with almost as many gates on its worst path as a ripple-carry adder. Why, and what follows for writing arithmetic in RTL?

  3. Why does a pipeline raise the throughput but not shorten the latency, and what limits the gain of more stages? Which signals must pass through the pipeline as well? What is retiming, and why does it complicate the equivalence check?

  4. Name the three components of the power consumption of a CMOS circuit, and write the formula of the switching power. Which levers reduce the dynamic and the static power, and why does a slower clock alone not save energy per operation?

  5. Why does a plain AND gate of the clock and an enable not work as a clock gate? Draw an integrated clock gate and its waveforms, and explain why it uses a latch. Why does clock gating save most of the power of a register whose enable is rarely high, but little when the enable is high in every cycle?

12.8 Clock Domains, Metastability, and Resets

  1. What is a clock domain, and when are two clocks synchronous or asynchronous? What is a clock domain crossing, why can static timing analysis not check it, and which SDC command removes the paths between two asynchronous clocks from the analysis?

  2. Explain metastability with the cross-coupled inverters of a latch and its time constant \(\tau\). Write the formula for the mean time between failures (MTBF) of a synchronizer, explain each term, and say why a synchronizer is designed for the slow corner.

  3. Draw a two-flip-flop synchronizer and explain why it raises the MTBF. Which rules must a synchronizer follow, and by which factor does a third flip-flop raise the MTBF?

  4. Why can a one-cycle pulse from a fast clock domain get lost in a slow one? Draw a pulse synchronizer and explain how it works. How far apart must two pulses be?

  5. Why can a bus whose bits change at the same time not cross through one synchronizer per bit? Name three ways to cross it, explain why Gray code works for counters and pointers, and describe a handshake.

  6. Draw an asynchronous FIFO. Why does each pointer exist in binary and in Gray code? How are the full and the empty flag computed, why can they be pessimistic, and why does the memory need no synchronizer?

  7. Why is the release of an asynchronous reset a clock domain crossing? What does a reset synchronizer do, how many does a design with several clock domains need, and why must the reset input itself be free of glitches?

12.9 Design for Test (DFT)

  1. Why must every manufactured die be tested? Name the three tests that a die can go through between the wafer and the shipment, and what each of them catches.

  2. What are yield, fault coverage, test coverage, and defect level? Write the model of Williams and Brown, and explain why a defect level of a few ppm needs a fault coverage close to 100 %.

  3. What is the stuck-at fault model? How many single stuck-at faults does a netlist with \(n\) fault sites have? What are equivalent and untestable faults?

  4. Name three kinds of production defects, the wrong behavior that each of them causes, and the fault model that describes it. What does IDDQ testing measure?

  5. Describe the three steps of finding a test for a stuck-at fault, and explain controllability and observability. How do the D-algorithm and a SAT solver on a miter show that a fault is untestable, and why do ATPG tools start with random vectors?

  6. What is scan design? Draw a scan flip-flop and a scan chain, and explain how scan turns the test of a sequential circuit into the test of a combinational one. What does scan cost, and how do you check that the scan insertion did not change the function?

  7. Describe the scan test sequence, including the chain test. How many clock cycles does a test of \(N\) patterns over a chain of \(L\) flip-flops take, and how can the test time be reduced? Why is the shift clock often slower than the functional clock?

  8. Name and explain at least four design rules for testability besides those for the scan chain itself. Why does a reset synchronizer in front of the registers break the scan chain, and how is it fixed?

  9. What do an at-speed test, a logic built-in self-test, a memory BIST, and boundary scan add to the scan test? Explain launch on capture, launch on shift, and aliasing.

12.10 The RTL-to-GDSII Flow with LibreLane

  1. What are the die and the core of a floorplan? How does the utilization set the size of the core, and why is the core not filled with cells completely? How are the rows, the power grid, and the pins arranged, and what does a denser core gain and cost?

  2. What do global placement, the repair of the design, and detailed placement do? Which limits does the repair of the design enforce, what happens to the timing of a net that exceeds them, and why does the reset net need the repair?

  3. What is a clock tree, and what is it used for? How does TritonCTS build an H-tree, and what is a dummy load?

  4. What changes in the timing analysis after clock tree synthesis, and why does the flow repair hold violations only after it? How does CTS treat a clock gate, and why do the paths into a divided clock violate hold?

  5. What do global and detailed routing do, and what is congestion? What is the antenna rule, and how is a violation fixed? Which cells does the fill insertion add to the rows after routing, and why?

  6. What does the signoff check? Explain parasitic extraction, the signoff STA in all corners, the IR drop analysis, DRC, and LVS, and say why the equivalence check runs again on the final netlist.

  7. How does the flow estimate the wires after placement, and why are these estimates optimistic? Why does the slow corner lose the most slack, and why can a setup margin for the timing repair close the timing where a delay-oriented synthesis does not?

  8. What does a padframe do? What do the IO cells, the core ring, the seal ring, and the metal fill add to a chip, and which steps does the Chip flow add to the Classic flow?

12.11 Calculation Problems

  1. Delay Table: Around an input slew of 0.2 ns and a load of 0.03 pF, the table cell_rise of a cell holds four entries: 0.10 ns at a slew of 0.1 ns and a load of 0.02 pF, 0.20 ns at 0.1 ns and 0.06 pF, 0.14 ns at 0.3 ns and 0.02 pF, and 0.26 ns at 0.3 ns and 0.06 pF. Compute the delay by linear interpolation, first along the load and then along the slew.

  2. Setup and Hold Slack: A path between two flip-flops on the same clock has a clock-to-output delay of 0.2 ns, a longest logic delay of 1.5 ns, a shortest logic delay of 0.02 ns, a setup time of 0.1 ns, and a hold time of 0.05 ns. The clock reaches the capturing flip-flop 0.1 ns later than the launching one, and the clock uncertainty is 0.1 ns for both checks. Compute the setup slack at a clock period of 2 ns, the minimum period, and the hold slack. Which check fails, does a slower clock help, and how do you fix it?

  3. Switching Power: The data nets of a block have a total capacitance of 20 pF and an average activity of 0.1 transitions per clock cycle, and its clock net has 2 pF. Compute the switching power of the data nets and of the clock net at 1.2 V and 250 MHz. By which factor does the switching power grow at 1.5 V and the same clock frequency?

  4. Synchronizer MTBF: A flip-flop has \(\tau\) = 100 ps and \(T_0\) = 20 ps, a clock-to-output delay of 0.2 ns, and a setup time of 0.1 ns. A signal that changes \(10^7\) times per second enters a domain clocked at 500 MHz through a two-flip-flop synchronizer. Compute the MTBF, the factor by which a third flip-flop raises it, and the MTBF with three flip-flops in years. Use \(e^{17} \approx 2.4 \cdot 10^7\) and 1 year \(\approx 3.2 \cdot 10^7\) s.

  5. Defect Level: A process has a yield of 90 %, and the test reaches a fault coverage of 98 %. Compute the defect level in ppm with the model of Williams and Brown, and the coverage that a defect level of 10 ppm needs. Use \(Y^x \approx 1 + x \ln Y\) for small \(x\), and \(\ln 0.9 \approx -0.105\).

  6. Test Vectors: A circuit computes \(y = ab + c\), with the internal net \(n = ab\). Find a test vector \((a, b, c)\) for \(n\) stuck-at-0, for \(a\) stuck-at-1, and for \(c\) stuck-at-0, and say for each how it excites and propagates the fault. Then show that the net \(bc\) stuck-at-0 in \(y = ab + \bar{a}c + bc\) is untestable.

  7. Scan Test Time: A design has 1000 flip-flops, and its test has 200 scan patterns, which the tester shifts at 20 MHz. How long does the scan test take without the chain test, with one chain, and how long with 10 chains of 100 flip-flops each?

  8. Gray Code: Write down the 3-bit Gray code of 0 to 7. Convert the binary value 1011 into Gray code, and the Gray code 1101 back into binary. A 4-bit binary counter steps from 0111 to 1000 while another clock domain samples it through one synchronizer per bit. Which values can the other domain see, and which with a Gray-coded counter?

12.12 Reading, Writing, and Fixing Code

  1. Find the Bugs: The following module should add d_i to an 8-bit sum in every clock cycle in which en_i is high and keep the sum otherwise. The sum wraps around at 256. Find the three mistakes. For each one, explain what Verilator or Yosys reports or which hardware results, and write the corrected module.

    module acc (
  input  logic       clk_i,
  input  logic       rst_ni,
  input  logic       en_i,
  input  logic [7:0] d_i,
  output logic [7:0] sum_o
);
  logic [7:0] sum_d, sum_q;

  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) sum_q = '0;
    else         sum_q = sum_d;
  end

  always_comb begin
    if (en_i) sum_d = sum_q + d_i;
  end

  assign sum = sum_q;
endmodule

  2. From VHDL to SystemVerilog: The following counter is written in the two-process style of VHDL, with cnt and next_cnt of type unsigned(2 downto 0). Translate it into a SystemVerilog module cnt3 with the ports clk_i, rst_ni, en_i, clr_i, and tc_o, an asynchronous active-low reset, and the two-process style with _d and _q. Why must the sensitivity list of cnt_logic contain all three signals, and what replaces it in SystemVerilog?

    reg_proc: process(rst_i, clk_i) is
begin
  if rst_i = '1' then
    cnt <= (others => '0');
  elsif rising_edge(clk_i) then
    cnt <= next_cnt;
  end if;
end process reg_proc;

cnt_logic: process(cnt, en_i, clr_i) is
begin
  next_cnt <= cnt;
  if clr_i = '1' then
    next_cnt <= (others => '0');
  elsif en_i = '1' then
    next_cnt <= cnt + 1;
  end if;
end process cnt_logic;

tc_o <= '1' when cnt = 7 else '0';

  3. Clock Enable Instead of a Divided Clock: The following code counts at half the clock frequency. Rewrite it with only one clock, an asynchronous active-low reset rst_ni, and a clock enable, so that the counter still advances at every second rising edge of clk_i. What does a simulation of the original show, since div_q has no reset, and why does your version not have this problem?

    always_ff @(posedge clk_i) begin
  div_q <= ~div_q;
end

always_ff @(posedge div_q) begin
  cnt_q <= cnt_q + 1'b1;
end

  4. Liberty Cell: The following excerpt describes a cell of the typical library, whose units are ns and pF.

    cell (sg13cmos5l_a21oi_1) {
  area : 9.072;
  pin (Y) {
    direction : "output";
    function : "!((A1*A2)+B1)";
    max_capacitance : 0.3;
    timing () {
      related_pin : "A1";
      timing_sense : negative_unate;
      timing_type : combinational;
      cell_rise (TIMING_DELAY_7x7ds1) { ... }
      cell_fall (TIMING_DELAY_7x7ds1) { ... }
    }
  }
  pin (A1) {
    direction : "input";
    capacitance : 0.00301392;
  }
}

    Draw the gate that the function describes. What does the timing sense of the arc from A1 to Y mean? How large is the cell in gate equivalents, if a 2-input NAND gate has 7.2576 µm²? What is the input capacitance of A1 in fF, and what happens when the output has to drive more than max_capacitance?

  5. Timing Report: The following report of OpenSTA shows the worst setup path of a block with an ideal clock of 1.25 ns.

    Startpoint: a_q (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
Endpoint: b_q (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
Path Group: clk
Path Type: max

  Delay    Time   Description
-----------------------------------------------------------
  0.000   0.000   clock clk (rise edge)
  0.000   0.000   clock network delay (ideal)
  0.000   0.000 ^ a_q/CLK (sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1)
  0.210   0.210 v a_q/Q (sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1)
  0.650   0.860 ^ u1/Y (sg13cmos5l_nor4_1)
  0.290   1.150 ^ u2/X (sg13cmos5l_mux2_1)
  0.000   1.150 ^ b_q/D (sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1)
          1.150   data arrival time

  1.250   1.250   clock clk (rise edge)
  0.000   1.250   clock network delay (ideal)
 -0.100   1.150   clock uncertainty
  0.000   1.150   clock reconvergence pessimism
          1.150 ^ b_q/CLK (sg13cmos5l_dfrbpq_1)
 -0.120   1.030   library setup time
          1.030   data required time
-----------------------------------------------------------
          1.030   data required time
         -1.150   data arrival time
-----------------------------------------------------------
         -0.120   slack (VIOLATED)

    Is the check met? Compute the minimum clock period of this path. Which cell takes the most time, and why is its rising output slow? Propose two fixes. Which lines of the two clock paths change if only set_propagated_clock is added to the constraints after clock tree synthesis, and why?

  6. Timing Constraints: Write the SDC constraints for a block with the clock input clk_i at 200 MHz, a clock transition of 0.1 ns, a clock uncertainty of 0.15 ns, input delays of 1.5 ns at all other inputs, output delays of 1.5 ns at all outputs, the cell sg13cmos5l_buf_2 with its output pin X as the driver of the inputs, and a load of 10 fF at the outputs, in the units of the library, ns and pF. Explain what each command tells the timing analysis.

  7. Clock Domain Crossing: req_a is a pulse of one cycle of the faster clock clk_a_i, and the following code takes it into the domain of clk_b_i. Find the three mistakes, and draw a corrected crossing.

    // domain A
assign req_a = start_a_i & ready_a_q;

// domain B
always_ff @(posedge clk_b_i or negedge rst_b_ni) begin
  if (!rst_b_ni) begin
    s1_q <= 1'b0;
    s2_q <= 1'b0;
  end else begin
    s1_q <= req_a;
    s2_q <= s1_q & en_b_i;
  end
end
